Some aspects of hip fracture management are already covered by NICE guidance and are
therefore outside the scope of this guideline.

To ensure comprehensive management and
continuity, the following NICE guidance should be referred to when developing a complete
programme of care for each patient:
• NICE technology appraisal guidance on preventing osteoporotic fragility fractures in
postmenopausal women (alendronate, denosumab, etidronate, risedronate, raloxifene,
strontium ranelate and teriparatide).

content:
This
would ideally be a multicentre trial including 3,000 participants in each arm.

This is
achievable given that there are about 70,000 to 75,000 hip fractures a year in the UK.

The study should have 3 arms that look at spinal anaesthesia versus spinal
anaesthesia plus sedation versus general anaesthesia; this would separate those with
regional anaesthesia from those with regional anaesthesia plus sedation.

The study
would also need to control for surgery, especially type of fracture, prosthesis and
grade of surgeon.

content:
How the recommendations might affect practice
The recommendations remain largely unchanged from the 2012 NICE guideline on
osteoporosis but risk assessment rates vary, particularly for people who have not had
a fragility fracture. These recommendations may raise awareness and increase the
number of people being assessed for fracture risk. If this is the case there may be
increased resource use related to risk assessment, dual-energy X‑ray absorptiometry
(DXA) scans, and treatment, but savings because of reduced fragility fractures in the
long term.

NICE has made a recommendation for research on using electronic health records to help
identify adults who should have a fragility fracture risk assessment.
Why the committee made no recommendations
No evidence was identified for electronic health records so the committee made this
recommendation for research. The committee agreed that electronic health records
have the potential to help make it easier to identify people at risk of fragility fracture
who may benefit from treatment.

How the recommendations might affect practice
Incorporating VFA scans into DXA scan appointments for men aged 70 and over and
women aged 60 and over will be a change in practice.

Currently, VFA is limited to
some groups of people or not used at all.

Additional staff time will also be needed to
carry out, review and report VFAs.

In most cases, additional scanning time should be
able to be accommodated within existing DXA slots but appropriate scheduling of
less mobile patients may be needed.

DXA capacity should therefore not be impacted.

content:
Where VFA is currently used, it will displace spinal imaging to look
for vertebral fracture at lower cost in some people.

But the population recommended
for VFA will be broader than that currently having spinal radiograph and a small
proportion of VFA results may need a subsequent spinal image when there is
uncertainty.

Overall, a net reduction in spinal images is anticipated.

Increased use of VFA in the NHS is expected to increase identification of vertebral
fractures, which are often missed in current practice.

content:
Most evidence on accuracy of DXA-based VFA scans uses older scanners and shows
low specificity. Recent scanners have increased image quality and resolution, which
should result in better accuracy (for both sensitivity and specificity) for detecting
vertebral fractures. So, the committee made a recommendation for research on the
accuracy of DXA-based VFA.
Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence review G:
diagnosing vertebral fractures with DXA-based VFA.

content:
Most of the evidence to assess fracture risk was on DXA scans and this is the method
used in current practice.

The evidence for other bone density assessment techniques
was limited and did not support a change to current practice.

Two studies found
possible utility using quantitative computed tomography (QCT) while a single study
found possible utility using radiofrequency echographic multi spectrometry (REMS),
an ultrasound-based bone density assessment technique, and the committee made
recommendations for research on REMS, DXA with trabecular bone score (TBS)
assessment and QCT.
